prize_parts.citation: for the proposal and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms confined at a magic wavelength allow frequency standards with uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B052 as the sole prize, credited to Katori and Ye. In answer to the chair's first question, what separates the lattice clock from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize is a specific physical idea. The magic-wavelength condition makes the optical trapping potential shift the upper and lower clock levels equally, so the trap does not perturb the transition to first order, and the atoms sit in the Lamb-Dicke regime with no first-order Doppler or recoil shift. That gives a large ensemble of neutral atoms interrogated in parallel, which is why the stability and the systematic evaluation at the 10^-18 level are reachable in practical times. The comb is the counting tool, and the ion clock uses one trapped ion with a different set of limits, so neither prize covers this scheme. The consequences are measured and not promised: independent laboratories on strontium and ytterbium reproduce the uncertainty, clocks have been compared over long links, and millimetre-scale gravitational redshift has been resolved. On timing, none of that depends on a decision about the second, so I see no scientific reason to wait. The credit is also the cleanest on the shortlist, since Katori proposed the scheme and Ye's group showed what it could deliver. Having read the full exchange, I find no objection to the merit of the physics, only objections about overlap, timing and the ranking of other candidates, and I have not seen evidence that changes my assessment of those.
statement.case_against: The overlap with earlier prizes remains the real weakness, and my answer to the chair depends on a citation that is narrow. If the citation reads as a general prize for optical clocks, the objections of Mehlig, Eriksson and Olsson would be right, so the wording must name the magic-wavelength lattice scheme and its demonstrated realisation. The two-name credit leaves out PTB, SYRTE, NIST and Tokyo contributors such as Takamoto, and a committee that thinks those contributions are inseparable would have to either narrow the citation or add a third name; I recall priority details from memory and cannot settle them from the supplied files. The redefinition of the second is still pending, which some members weigh as a timing reason. Finally, the clock is an instrument achievement and a reader could ask whether it is a discovery in the statutory sense, which is why the citation must say what is new in physics terms.

responses.point: Mehlig accepts that the lattice clock is a distinct step from the comb and has moved it up as his first alternative, but still regards it as a superb instrument and a precision improvement, whereas B044 opened a qualitatively new class of experiments, and says he would be comfortable with either if attribution certainty is preferred.
responses.response: I am glad the comb overlap no longer carries your seventh place, and I accept that the lattice clock is an instrument. But I do not think the precision-improvement label fits: the magic-wavelength scheme is a new way of controlling a many-atom quantum system so that the environment does not change the transition, and the clock then tests physics, for example the redshift and constants. Your B044 is my second choice and I regard the Bloch-Greiner experiment and the Jaksch-Zoller proposal as one coherent story. The difference for me is that the third name is unresolved: Zoller or Esslinger is a choice the supplied credit cannot settle, and Zoller appears on B009 as well. You say you would be comfortable with B052 if the committee wants attribution certainty, and that is precisely the criterion that members have all described as decisive, so I ask you to weigh it as part of the scientific case and not as a concession.

responses.point: Olsson argues that the measurement-limited, broad-downstream-use criterion cuts at least as sharply for aberration correction, that the pending redefinition of the second is a timing argument that does not apply to an instrument used for twenty years, and that the 2005 and 2012 overlaps should be addressed in the citation.
responses.response: I agree the overlap should be answered in the citation and I have done that above. Where I differ is on the comparison. Aberration correction is a strong invention and the confirmation is beyond doubt, but the clock changes what can be tested about nature: the lattice scheme produced a measurement of time dilation across millimetres, bounds on drifting constants and a route to a new definition of the second. I would also not let the redefinition be a reason for either of us: I do not tie B052 to it, so it is not a timing argument against B011 either. The point on which I agree with you is that the STEM corrector lineage (Krivanek, Dellby) lies outside Rose, Haider and Urban, so B011 has an attribution cost of its own, which is of the same kind as the PTB and SYRTE issue for the clock but, in my view, less easily answered by wording, because the TEM and STEM lines are two corrector designs and not one idea with several demonstrations.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B021 as a new class of matter and a larger conceptual step than a precision invention, would frame the citation around the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 invariant, and would accept B052 without objection if clean credit is preferred.
responses.response: I take seriously that B021 is a larger conceptual step, and it remains my third choice. A narrower citation on the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 invariant does make the 3D omissions easier to defend, and I thank you for that. My remaining difficulty is the one Olsson and Mehlig also raised: the HgTe experiment of Molenkamp followed the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, so a citation to the observation cannot be written without that theory in it, and a trio that omits it would be hard to defend. Since you also say you would accept B052 on clean credit, we may be closer than the first-choice count suggests. I would ask whether you consider a 2D-only citation sufficient to overcome the BHZ problem. If you do, I would like to hear why the experiment can be credited without the proposal, but I do not see it from the supplied names and I have not changed my view.

responses.point: Kroll counters that the clock tests physics and not only serves as a tool, and has asked whether his research stay in John Hall's laboratory, the group in which Jun Ye trained, calls for a disclosure or recusal on B052.
responses.response: I agree with your argument that the clock is a test of physics, and I think it is the strongest answer to the instrument objection. On your disclosure question, I would say it should be recorded but it is not in itself a recusal reason: you have no documented joint work with Katori or Ye, and a stay in a laboratory that Ye later joined is a thin tie compared with the physics. I would only add that, since you and I both rank B052 first, we should be the members who state most carefully what the citation does not cover, namely the laser stabilisation and comparison work and the other lattice-clock groups.

uncertainties: Whether a citation tied narrowly to the magic-wavelength lattice scheme is enough to persuade members who see the clock as an increment on the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Whether Takamoto, PTB, SYRTE or NIST contributors are inseparable from the credited pair; I recall priority details from memory and have not verified them here.
Whether members who prefer B021, B044, B056 or B011 will accept B052 as the sole prize, and whether a two-part prize is possible within three names, which I think it is not without splitting credit.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second weighs for some members as a timing argument, which I do not accept but cannot rule out for others.
My ranking of the alternatives B044 and B021 stays provisional, because the Zoller versus Esslinger choice and the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are not resolved by the supplied names.
statement.conflict_note: No change. I have no documented collaboration with Katori or Ye, and none of my documented connections (Ingvar Lindgren's group, Anne L'Huillier and the Lund attosecond group, Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti, Indelicato) appear among the credited names in the shortlist, including B044, B021 and B009 where I list fallbacks. I share the atomic physics field with the lattice-clock work, which is expertise and not a conflict, and I see no need to recuse from any shortlisted item. I note that Kroll's disclosure on B052 involves a laboratory tie and not a collaboration, and I do not regard it as disqualifying.
